title: A one-byte randomblob corruption is a no-op 1 run in 256, so the corrupt-on-disk test flakes and the harness cannot tell a no-op from a result
description:
FILED 2026-09-29 from WCLI-57 and CORRECTED the same session, after its own reproduction was found to measure the probe rather than the product. The correction is recorded rather than applied silently, because the first version of this record asserted a toolchain defect that does not exist.

WHAT THE FIRST VERSION SAID, AND HOW IT GOT IN. It said a bare autocommit write on a short-lived bun:sqlite connection can silently not land, roughly 1 in 300-800 times, and offered as evidence a set of local probes plus a control with no Ward code in it. Every one of those probes used the failing test's own mutation - UPDATE ... SET body = randomblob(length(body)) on a ONE-BYTE body - and detected a non-landing write by comparing the row's bytes before and after. A one-byte randomblob reproduces the original byte 1 time in 256, so 1 run in 256 the row is LEGITIMATELY unchanged and the detector called it a lost write. The measured rates (0.25-0.58%) sit on 1/256 = 0.39%, which is what the numbers said all along.

THE DECISIVE MEASUREMENT (2000 iterations per variant, same shape, only the written expression differs):
- randomblob(length(body)) on a one-byte body: 5 unchanged rows (0.25%; 1/256 predicts 7).
- randomblob(8): 0 unchanged.
- zeroblob(1), which can never equal the seed byte: 0 unchanged.
Two earlier discriminators are consistent with this and were misread as evidence of loss: the file on disk was byte-identical after the "lost" writes (a collision leaves it identical, correctly), and a "retry" always landed (the retry is drawn again, so it collides again only 1/256 of the time).

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE.
- The store's behaviour was correct in every observation: with the ciphertext genuinely unchanged, decrypting the OLD ciphertext succeeds and the read legitimately returns the plaintext. Nothing fails closed because nothing was corrupted.
- That is exactly the CI failure: run 36592695262, the vault-store case asserting that a ciphertext modified on disk fails authentication, Expected vault_authentication_failed, Received not-a-ward-error - and not-a-ward-error is what the helper returns when the call does NOT throw, which is the correct outcome for a read of an uncorrupted vault.
- Ward's own write path lost 0 writes in 4000 create+mutate+read cycles (about 8000 writes), which at the rates this record originally claimed would have been a near-certain observation of loss. It measured nothing of the kind, and the earlier 0/400 reading was correct.

THE REAL DEFECT, which is a test-harness defect and still worth fixing: a security-relevant case - "a modified ciphertext on disk fails authentication" - asserts its outcome on a premise that holds only 255 times in 256, so it reddens about 0.4% of suite runs and, worse, cannot distinguish "the corruption was a no-op" from "the reader failed to notice a corrupt vault". The second reading is the dangerous one: the same shape would let the case pass while testing nothing if a future edit changed which value is written.

SCOPE OF THE FIX: make the corruption real by construction at that site, and make the shared helper refuse to proceed when a mutation changed nothing, so no future site can silently assert on an uncorrupted file. The store, the vault format and the crypto are NOT implicated and need no change.

acceptanceCriteria.text: The vault-store case that requires a modified ciphertext to fail authentication changes the ciphertext by construction rather than by chance, so its premise holds on every run rather than 255 runs in 256.

A mutation helper that changes nothing on disk fails loudly and names itself as a harness fault instead of letting the caller assert on an unchanged vault, proven by a deliberate no-op mutation that the detector catches.

Every other case in the suite that mutates the vault on disk and then asserts an outcome is checked against the same premise - that its mutation really changes the file - and any that does not is fixed or recorded with its reason.

plan: 1. Make the vault-store ciphertext case corrupt the value by construction instead of by chance, so its premise holds on every run.
2. Give the raw mutation helper an assertion that its mutation changed the file, failing loudly as a harness fault, and prove the detector with a deliberate no-op.
3. Sweep the other raw-mutation sites against the same premise; the helper enforces it at every call site, and the suite run is what shows each one really changes the file.
implementationNotes:
FIXED 2026-09-29, in this pull request.

THE SITE. The vault-store case asserting that a modified ciphertext fails authentication now corrupts by construction: it reads the ciphertext, flips every bit of its first byte, and writes it back, so the value cannot equal what was there. The old form rewrote it with randomblob(length(ciphertext)), and this plaintext is one byte, so the rewrite was a no-op 1 run in 256.

THE HELPER. withRaw, the one path every raw mutation in that file goes through, now asserts its own premise: it reads the file before and after the mutation and throws a message naming itself as a harness fault when the bytes are identical. A file that did not exist before and does now counts as changed, which is the shape the three planting sites use. The throw is deliberate rather than a retry - retrying a colliding random value until it differs would hide exactly the defect that was found here, and the point is that a no-op must never reach an assertion.

BOTH HALVES PROVEN, and the second is the one that matters:
- The detector fires on a deliberate no-op: a new case calls the helper with a statement that changes nothing and requires the harness error. Green.
- At the real site, with the corruption mutated back to a no-op, the case now fails LOUDLY with the harness message rather than reading the old plaintext and reporting that the reader missed a corrupt vault. Measured, then reverted. Before this change that same input produced the false reading instead.

THE SWEEP (AC3). Every raw-mutation site in the file goes through the helper, so the premise is enforced at each of them rather than eyeballed: the suite passing is what shows each mutation really changes the file. The two remaining randomblob uses in test/fixtures/vault-store-worker.ts are not affected - one also sets revision = revision + 1, which changes the row whatever the random byte is, and the other inserts a 1 MB blob.

CHECKS: 667 pass, 0 fail across the suite; vault-store.test.ts alone 42 pass; layer check 0 violations; eval structural check OK; the 3 lint warnings are the pre-existing ones. The store, the vault format and the crypto are untouched: this was a test premise, and the reader was right in every observation.
